title: De Gratia Christi Et De Peccato Originali Contra Pelagium Et Coelestinum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa046.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: et hæc de lege ac doctriua, seu de divina revelatione ac de chrisli exemiio, quæ ad doctrinam aeque revocautur, aut de peccatorum reniissione interpretari posse demonstrat, nec apparere tmnino, an vere cbrislianam gratiam, id est, adjutorium hene agendi adjunctum naturae atque doctrinæ per inspirationem flagrantissimæ et lumiuosissimae charitatis agnos -aL Pelagius: qui postremo Ambrosium, tantopere ab ipso laudatum, praeclara quaedam in commendationem divinae gratiae dicentem audire jubetur.
passages.english: and he shows that these too can be interpreted as referring to the law and teaching, or to divine revelation and the example of Christ, which are equally reduced to teaching, or to the remission of sins; and that it does not appear at all whether Pelagius acknowledges truly Christian grace, that is, a help for acting well added to nature and teaching through the inspiration of a most ardent and most luminous charity. Finally Pelagius is bidden to listen to Ambrose, so highly praised by him, as he says certain splendid things in commendation of divine grace.
passages.notes: This is from an editorial summary (argument) of the work, not Augustine's text. Scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'doctriua' for 'doctrina', 'chrisli exemiio' for 'Christi exemplo', 'agnos -aL' for 'agnoscat').

passages.original: Charitas autem Dei non per legem diO'usa est in cordibus nostris, sed per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis (Id. v, 5). Proinde per legem gratia demonstratur, ut lex per gratiam compleatur. Quid enim juvat Pelagium, quia dlversis verbis eamdem rem dicit, ut non intelligatur in lege atque doctrina gratiam constituere, qua possibilitatem naturae asserit adjuvari? Quantum autem existimo, ideo veretur intelligi, quia damnavit eos qui dicunt gratiam Dei et adjutorium non ad singulos actus dari, sed in libero arbitrio esse, vel in lege atque doctrina : et tamen latere se putat, cum aliis atque aliis locutionibus versat significationem legis atque doctrinæ.
passages.english: But the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts not through the law, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). Accordingly grace is pointed out through the law, so that the law may be fulfilled through grace. For what does it help Pelagius that he says the same thing in different words, so that he may not be understood to locate in law and teaching the grace by which he asserts that the capacity of nature is helped? As far as I judge, he fears being understood in this way because he condemned those who say that the grace and help of God is not given for individual acts, but lies in free choice, or in law and teaching; and yet he thinks he escapes notice when he turns over the meaning of law and teaching in one expression after another.

passages.original: Quorum autem sit fides, et quibus persuadetur ut ad eum veniant, satis ipse demonstravit, ubi ait, Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum: et paulo post, cum de non credentibus loqueretur, Dixi, inquit, vobis, quia nemo potest venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo (Joan. VI, 44, 66). Hanc debet Pelagius gratiam confiteri, si vult non solum vocari, Terum etiam esse christianus.
passages.english: But whose the faith is, and who are persuaded to come to him, he himself showed clearly enough where he says, "No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him"; and a little later, when he was speaking of those who did not believe, he says, "I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father" (John 6:44, 66). This is the grace Pelagius ought to confess, if he wishes not only to be called, but also to be, a Christian.

passages.original: Si cnim solum posse nostrum hac gratia juvaretur, ita diceret Dominus : Omnis qui audivit a Patre et didicit, potest venire ad me. Non autem ita dixit: sed, Omnis qui audivit, inquit, a Patre et didicit, venit ad me. Venire posse in natura ponit Pelagius, vel etiam , ut modo dicere coepit, in gratia, qualemlibet cam sentiat, < qua ipsa, > ut dicit, < possibilitas adjuvatur: » vcnire autem jam in voluntate et opere est. Non est autcm consequens ut qui potest venire, etiam veniat, nisi id voluerit atque fecerit.
passages.english: For if only our ability were helped by this grace, the Lord would have spoken thus: "Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned, can come to me." But he did not speak thus; rather he says, "Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned, comes to me." Pelagius places the ability to come in nature, or even, as he has lately begun to say, in grace, whatever he takes it to be, "by which," as he says, "the capacity itself is helped"; but coming now lies in will and deed. And it does not follow that one who can come actually comes, unless he has willed and done it.

passages.original: sed, ul bonum faciatis (II Cor. XIII, 7). Quoniam de quibus scriptum est, Quotquot enim Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei (Rom. VIII, 14) ; profecto ut agant quod bonum est, ab illo aguntur qui bonus est. Quomodo dicit Pelagius, cQuod bene loqui possumus, Dei cst: quod bene loquimur, nostrum est ; » cum dicat Dominus, Spiritus Patris vestri eat qui loquitur in vobis ? Nequo cnim ait, Non vos estis qui dedistis vobis bene posse loqui : sed ait, Non vos eatis qui loquimini (Matth.
passages.english: but, "that you may do good" (2 Cor. 13:7). For of those of whom it is written, "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God" (Rom. 8:14), surely, in order that they may do what is good, they are led by him who is good. How does Pelagius say, "That we can speak well is God's; that we speak well is ours," when the Lord says, "It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you"? For he does not say, "It is not you who gave yourselves the ability to speak well"; but he says, "It is not you who speak" (Matt.
passages.notes: Latin 'aguntur' means both 'are led' and 'are driven/made to act'; Augustine plays on 'agant' (do) and 'aguntur'. Citation completed in the following context (Matt. 10:20).

passages.original: CAPUT XXXII. — 35. Sed ab his litteris Pelagius ad fidei suae librura (a) vult transire lectorem , cujus vobis ' commemorationem fecit: in quo ea de quibus nun interrogabatur, multa disseruit. Sed nos de quibus agimus cum illis, ipsa videamus. Cum enim ab unitate Trinitatis usque ad resurrectionem carnis, quod ab illo nemo quærebat, disputationem quantam voluit terminasset : c Et Baptisma, > inquit, < unum tenemus, quod iisdem Sacramenti verbis in infantibus, quibus etiam in majoribus, dicimus esse cclebrandum.
passages.english: CHAPTER 32. — 35. But from this letter Pelagius wants to send the reader over to his book on his faith, of which he made mention to you; in which he discussed at length many things about which he was not being questioned. But let us look at those very things which are at issue between us and them. For when he had completed as long a discussion as he wished, from the unity of the Trinity up to the resurrection of the flesh, which no one was asking of him, he says: "We also hold one Baptism, which we say must be celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults."

passages.original: CAPUT XLIII. — 47. « Beatus, > inquit, t Ambrosius episcopus, in cujus præcipue libris Romana elucet fides, qui scriptorum inter Latinos flos quidam spe- clusus enituit, cujus fidem et purissimum in Scripturis sensum, ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere.
passages.english: CHAPTER XLIII. — 47. "The blessed bishop Ambrose," he says, "in whose books above all the Roman faith shines out, who has shone forth as a kind of flower among the Latin writers, whose faith and most pure understanding in the Scriptures not even an enemy has dared to criticise."
passages.notes: "spe- clusus" is a garbled scan, probably for "speciosus" ("a kind of beautiful flower"). The translation follows the sense without that word.

passages.original: CAPUT XLV. — 49. Ipsam denique pœnitentiam, qua In procul dubio voluntas agit, Domini misericordia et adjutorio ficri ut agatur, in nono 1 ejusdem operis libro beatus dicit Ambrosius, ita loquens : < Bonæ lacrymæ, quæ culpam lavaut. DtniqHe quos Jesus respicit, plorant *. Negavit primo Petrus, et non tevit, quia non respexerat Dominus : negavit secunda, non flevit, quia adhuc non respexerat Dominus : negavit et tertio, respexit Jesus, et ille amarissime flevit I (Lib. 10, n. 89, ad Luc. XXII, Ci). Legant isti Evangelium, et videant Dominum Jesum tunc intus fuisse, cum a sacerdotum principibus audiretur : apostolum vero Petrum foris et dcorsum in atrio cum servis ad focum nunc sedentem, nunc stantem, sicu!
passages.english: CHAPTER XLV. — 49. Finally, the blessed Ambrose says in the ninth book of the same work that repentance itself, in which the will is without doubt at work, comes about by the mercy and help of the Lord, so that it may be performed. He speaks thus: "Good are the tears that wash away guilt. Indeed, those on whom Jesus looks weep. Peter denied the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked [at him]; he denied the second time and did not weep, because the Lord had still not looked [at him]; he denied the third time too, Jesus looked, and he wept most bitterly" (Book 10, n. 89, on Luke 22:61). Let these men read the Gospel and see that the Lord Jesus was then inside, when he was being heard by the chief priests, while the apostle Peter was outside and below in the courtyard with the servants by the fire, now sitting, now standing, as
passages.notes: The text says the ninth book, but the reference given is to Book 10 of Ambrose's commentary on Luke. The passage breaks off mid-sentence ("sicut"), and the sentence continues in the following text. Scanning errors corrected: "lavaut" read as "lavant", "DtniqHe" as "Denique", "tevit" as "flevit", "dcorsum" as "deorsum".

passages.original: 50. Item in eodem libro idem sanctus Ambrosius: < Nam si Petrus, > inquit (Lib. 10, n. 91, ad Luc. XXII), < lapsus est, qui dixit, Etsi alii scandalizati fuerint, ego v non scandalizabor (Matth. XXVI, 33);quis alius jure de < se praesumat? Denique David quia dixerat, Ego dixi < in mea abundantia, Non movebor in œternum ; suam < sibi jactantiam obfuisse profitetur, dicens, Avertisti t faciem tuam, et factus sum conturbatus » (Psal. XXIX, 7, 8). Audiat iste tantum virum docentem , imitetur credentem, cujus doctrinam fidem que laudavit. Audial humiliter, imitetur fideliter : non de se pertinaciter præsumat, ne percat. Quid in eo pelago vult mergi Pelagius, unde per petram liberatus est Petrus ?
passages.english: 50. Likewise in the same book the same holy Ambrose says (Book 10, no. 91, on Luke 22): "For if Peter fell, who said, 'Even if others are scandalized, I will not be scandalized' (Matt. 26:33), who else may rightly presume on himself? Finally David, because he had said, 'I said in my abundance, I shall not be moved for ever,' confesses that his boasting harmed him, saying, 'You turned away your face, and I became troubled'" (Ps. 29:7-8). Let this man listen to so great a man teaching, let him imitate him believing, whose teaching and faith he praised. Let him listen humbly, let him imitate faithfully; let him not presume stubbornly on himself, lest he perish. Why does Pelagius want to be drowned in that sea from which Peter was freed through the rock?
passages.notes: Wordplay in the Latin: pelago (sea) / Pelagius, petram (rock) / Petrus.

passages.original: > Numquid aliquis dicere audebit, nondum esse religiosum, < qui currit ad Dominum, et ab eo se regi cupit, et voluntatem suam ex ejus voluntate suspendit, et qui ei adhærendo jugiter, unus, secundum Aposlolum, cum eo fit spiritus > (Pelagii verba, supra, n. 24) ? At hoc totum tam magnum religiosi hominis opus, Pelagius « non > dicit «effici, nisi arbitrii libertate. u Contra autem beatus Ambrosius ipsius tam excellenter ore laudatus, « Dominus Deus-, I inquit, « quem dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit. > Ergo ut cwrrat ad Dominum, et ab eo se regi cupiat, suamque voluntatem ex ejus voluntate suspendat, eique adhnerendo jugiter unus, secundum Apostolum, cum eo fiat spiritus (I Cor. vi, 17), Deus quem vult religiosum facil: ct hoc totum homo nisi religiosus non facit. Quapropter nisi a Deo fiat, ut hoc faciat, quis hoc facit ?
passages.english: Will anyone dare to say that he is not yet religious "who runs to the Lord, and desires to be ruled by him, and makes his own will depend on his will, and who by cleaving to him constantly becomes, according to the Apostle, one spirit with him" (Pelagius' words, above, no. 24)? Yet this whole so great work of a religious man Pelagius says "is not brought about except by freedom of choice." But against this, blessed Ambrose, so excellently praised by Pelagius's own mouth, says, "The Lord God calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he wills." Therefore, that a man may run to the Lord, and desire to be ruled by him, and make his own will depend on his will, and by cleaving to him constantly become, according to the Apostle, one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17), God makes religious whom he wills; and a man does not do all this unless he is religious. Therefore, unless it is brought about by God that he does this, who does it?

passages.original: Sed quia ista quæstio, ubi de arbitrio voluntatis et Dci gratia disputatur, ita est ad discernendum difficilis, ut quando defenditur liberum arbitrium, negari Dci gratia videatur; quando autem asseritur Dei gratia, liberum arbitrium putetur auferri : potest Pelagius ita sc latebris obscuritatis hujus involvere, ut etiam iis quæ a sancto Ambrosio conscripta posuimus, consentire se dicat; et ea se quoque sentire proclamet, semperque sensisse; atque ita singula coneture exponere, ut etiam ejus sententiæ convenire credantur. Quapropter quantum attinet ad istam de divina gratia ct adjutorio quaestioncm, tria illa quæ apertissime distinxit auendile : posse, velle, esse I;
passages.english: But this question, where free choice of the will and the grace of God are debated, is so difficult to settle that when free choice is defended, the grace of God seems to be denied, and when the grace of God is asserted, free choice is thought to be taken away. For that reason Pelagius can wrap himself in the hiding-places of this obscurity. He could say that he agrees even with the passages written by Saint Ambrose that we have set out, and proclaim that he too holds them and has always held them. He could try to explain each of them in such a way that they are believed to agree with his own view as well. Therefore, as far as this question of divine grace and help is concerned, attend to those three things which he distinguished most clearly: to be able, to will, to be;
passages.notes: "auendile" is a corrupt scan, read as "attendite" ("attend"). "esse" ("to be") is glossed in the following text as "actionem" ("action"), so the third term means actually doing.

passages.original: Attendat sanc iste in eodem ipso loco, uude hoc Ambrosianum testimonium, quod ci placebat, assampsit, etiam illud eum dixisse, quod i ab initio esse immaculatum 1, humanæ impossibile sit Daturæ : < ubi omnino illam naturalem possibilitatem, quam Pelagius non vult fideliter respicere pcccato esse vitiatam, et ideo jactanter extollit, enervem infirmamque testatur venerandus Ambrosius : procul dubio contra islius voluntatem, sed non contra apostolicam veritatem, ubi legilur, Fuimus et nos aliquan-do nutura filii ira, sicut et cœteri (Ephes. u, 3). Ipsa est enim per peceatum primi hominis, quod ex libero ejus venit arbitrio, vitiata ct damnata natura;
passages.english: Let this man surely attend to the fact that in that very same passage from which he took this testimony of Ambrose that pleased him, [Ambrose] also said that "to be spotless from the beginning" is impossible for human nature; where the venerable Ambrose testifies that that natural capacity, which Pelagius will not faithfully regard as vitiated by sin and therefore boastfully exalts, is entirely feeble and weak: doubtless against this man's wish, but not against apostolic truth, where we read, "We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest" (Eph. 2:3). For it is that very nature that was vitiated and condemned through the sin of the first man, which came from his free choice;

passages.original: ostendit Augustinus, Pelagium in quæstione de originali peccato ac de parvulorum Baptismate, nihil reipsa dissentire a discipulo ipsius cœlestio, qui peccatum originale confiteri nolens, vel etiam aperte negare ausus, Carthagine Lrius, ac postea Romae, episcopalibusjudiciis damnatus est.
passages.english: Augustine shows that Pelagius, on the question of original sin and the baptism of infants, in reality differs in nothing from his disciple Caelestius, who, unwilling to confess original sin, or even daring openly to deny it, was condemned by episcopal judgements first at Carthage and afterwards at Rome.
passages.notes: Editorial summary of Book 2, not Augustine's text. 'Lrius' read as 'prius' (first).

passages.original: CAPUT VI. — 6. Attendite itaque quid Coelestius apertissime dixerit, et ibi videbitis quid vobis Pelagius occultaverit. Coelestius quippe adjungit, et dicit: < In remissionem autem peccatoruM baptizandos infantes, non idcirco diximus, ut peccatum ex traduce firmare videamur : quod longe a catholico sensu alienum est.
passages.english: CHAPTER VI. — 6. So pay attention to what Caelestius said most openly, and there you will see what Pelagius concealed from you. For Caelestius adds, saying: "But we have not said that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order that we may seem to affirm sin by transmission, which is far removed from the catholic sense.
passages.notes: "ex traduce" refers to the transmission of sin by propagation from parents (traducianism). The quotation from Caelestius continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: Quoniam neque per mortem vel prævaricationem Ad;e omne genus hominum moriatur, neque per resurrectionem Christi omne genus hominum resurgat. Quoniam sanctus episcopus Augustinus adversus discipulos ejus in Sicilia respondit Hilario ad subjecta capitula , scribens libram (a) in quo ista continentur : Posse , bominem sine peccato esse, si velit : Infantes, etsi non baptizentur, habere vitam æternam : Divites baptizatos, nisi omnibus abrenuntient, si quid boni visi fuerint facere, non reputari illis, neque regnum Dei .
passages.english: That neither does the whole human race die through the death or transgression of Adam, nor does the whole human race rise again through the resurrection of Christ. That the holy bishop Augustine, against his disciples in Sicily, replied to Hilary on the appended headings, writing a book in which these things are contained: that a human being can be without sin if he wills; that infants, even if they are not baptised, have eternal life; that rich people who have been baptised, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with any good they may seem to do, nor [can they have] the kingdom of God.
passages.notes: The final clause is completed in the following text ("posse eos habere", "can they have"). "(a)" is an editorial footnote mark and has been left out.

passages.original: 19. Quomodo autcm Pelagius obrepere tentaverit ad fallendum etiam Apostolicæ Sedis episcopale judicium in bac ipsa quæstione de Baptismate parvulorum, diligenter attendite. In litteris enim quas Romam misit ad beatæ memoriæ papam Innocentium, quoniam in corpore eum non invenerunt, et saneto papæ Zosimo datae sunt, atque ad nos inde directæ, dicit se ab bominibus infamari, quod neget parvulis Baptismi sacramentum, et absque redemptione Christi aliquibus coelorum regna promittat.
passages.english: 19. But observe carefully how Pelagius tried to creep in so as to deceive even the episcopal judgement of the Apostolic See on this very question of the baptism of little children. For in the letter which he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, which, since they did not find him in the body, was given to the holy Pope Zosimus and sent on from there to us, he says that he is defamed by people [as one] who denies the sacrament of baptism to little children and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without the redemption of Christ.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected (autcm, bac, saneto, bominibus). "Since they did not find him in the body" means Innocent had died before the letter arrived.

passages.original: CAPUT XXVI. — 50. Non igitur, sicut Pelagius et ejus discipuli, tempora dividamus, dicentes, Primum vixisse justos homines ex natura, deinde sub lege, tertio sub gratia. Ex natura, scilicet ab Adam tam longa actatc, qua Icx nonduin crat data.
passages.english: CHAPTER XXVI. — 50. Let us not, then, divide the times as Pelagius and his disciples do, saying that righteous people lived first by nature, then under the law, thirdly under grace. By nature, that is, from Adam through that long age in which the law had not yet been given.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (actatc, Icx nonduin crat = aetate, lex nondum erat).

passages.original: — 47.Scd jani etiam istum conclusuri librum, oportere arbitramur, ut Ambrosium anstitem Dei, cujus inter latinæ linguæ scriptores ecclesiasticos pra cipue Pelagius integerrimam fidem prædicat, sicut de gratia fecimus (a), ita ct de peccato originali, in quo delendo ipsa gratia evidentius commendatur, calumniosæ istorum loquacitati respondere faciamus. In co opere quod scripsitde Resurrectione sanctus Ambrosius : < Lapsus sum, i inquit, in Adam, de paradiso ejectus in Adam, mortuus in Adam : quem non revocat 2 nisi me in Adam invenerit, ut in ilio culpæ obnoxium , morti debitum, ita in Christo justificatum > (Lib. de Fide Ressurectionis). Item scribens contra Novatianos ait : < Omnes homines sub peccato nascimur, quoram ipse ortus in vitio est, sicut habes lectum, dicente David, Ecce iii iniquitatibus conceptus sum, et in delicli. peperii me mater mea ( Psal. L, 7 ). Ideo Pauli caro corpus mortis erat, sicut ipse ait : Quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus ( Rom. VII, 24 ) ? Christi autem caro damnavit peccatum, quod nascendo non sensit. quod moriendo crucilixil; ut in carne nostra esset justificatio per gratiam, ubi crat ante colluvio per culpam > ( Lib. i de Pœnitentia, cap. i, vel 3). hem idem Ipse cum exponeret Isaiam prophetam loquens de Christo : < Idco, > inquit, < et quasi homo per universa tentaius cst, et in similitudine bominum cancla sustinuit : sed quasi de Spiritu natus abstinuit a peccato (Hebr. IV, 15). Omnis enim homo mendax ( Psal. cxv, 2) ; et nemo sine peccato, nisi unus Deus.
passages.english: — 47. But now, as we are about to close this book as well, we think it right to make Ambrose, the bishop of God, answer the slanderous talkativeness of these men. Among the church writers of the Latin tongue, it is he above all whose faith Pelagius proclaims as most sound. As we did concerning grace, so we will make him answer concerning original sin, in the blotting out of which grace itself is more clearly commended. In the work which Saint Ambrose wrote on the Resurrection he says: "I fell in Adam, I was cast out of paradise in Adam, I died in Adam. He does not call me back unless he has found me in Adam, so that as in him I was liable to guilt and owed to death, so in Christ [I am] justified" (Book on Faith in the Resurrection). Likewise, writing against the Novatianists, he says: "All of us human beings are born under sin, and our very origin is in fault, as you have read, when David says, Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me (Ps. 50:7). Therefore Paul's flesh was a body of death, as he himself says: Who will deliver me from the body of this death? (Rom. 7:24). But the flesh of Christ condemned sin, which he did not experience in being born, [and] which he crucified in dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace where before there was filth through guilt" (On Repentance, Book 1, chapter 1 or 3). Likewise the same man, when expounding the prophet Isaiah, speaking of Christ, says: "Therefore, as a man, he was tempted in all things, and in the likeness of men he endured all things; but as born of the Spirit he abstained from sin (Heb. 4:15). For every man is a liar (Ps. 115:2), and no one is without sin except God alone."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "crucilixil" read as "crucifixit", "hem" as "Item", "cancla" as "cuncta". The "(a)" and stray numerals are footnote marks and have been left out.

passages.original: 48. liis tamen verbis bominis Dei, quem tanto praeconio ipse laudavit Pelagius, contradicit, et dicit, < sicut sine virtute, ita nos sine vitio procreari. > Quid igitur restat, nisi aut istum Pelagius suum damnet errorem, aut euin sic Anabrosinm laudasse poeniteat ? Sed quia ista secundum catholicam fidem beatus Ambrosius, ut episcopus catholicus, est locutus;
passages.english: 48. Yet Pelagius contradicts these words of the man of God, whom he himself praised with such high commendation, and says that "just as we are procreated without virtue, so [we are procreated] without vice." What then remains, except that either Pelagius condemn this error of his, or regret having praised Ambrose in this way? But since the blessed Ambrose, as a catholic bishop, spoke these things according to the catholic faith,
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (liis = His, bominis, euin, Anabrosinm = Ambrosium). The sentence continues beyond the passage.
